title: Coordination services: ZooKeeper and etcd
subtitle: ZooKeeper and etcd keep a small amount of critical data that every node must agree on. Learn what they give you, where they break, and what not to put in them.

c.v: On 28 October 2021, Roblox engineers saw that Vault was slow and one Consul server had high CPU load. Players were still fine.
Roblox runs over 18,000 servers. Consul gave them
. Nomad and Vault both depended on it.
So when Consul was sick, services could not find each other. No new containers could start, and no secrets could be read. Roblox wrote: "the system failed because Consul was a
Writes to Consul's key-value store usually took under 300 ms at the median. Now they took 2 seconds.
The team replaced hardware. Later they shut down the whole cluster and restored a snapshot from before the outage. Neither fixed it.

There were two causes. A new Consul streaming feature caused contention under very high read and write load. And a usage pattern that arose during the incident hit a slow path in BoltDB, the store under Consul's
log. One log store was 4.2 GB but held only 489 MB of real data.

Monitoring also depended on Consul, so the team was partly blind while they debugged. Afterwards they split some critical services into their own Consul clusters. They also began moving data out of the key-value store. Some services had used it "as a convenient place to store data".

ZooKeeper lists what this store is for: configuration, naming, synchronization and group membership.

It is not a database. ZooKeeper "was not designed to be a general database or large object store". Its data is usually measured in kilobytes.
It works best when reads outnumber writes by about 10 to 1.
A coordination service holds the few facts your whole fleet must agree on. Keep that data small and slow-changing. Every extra use you add is one more thing that breaks when it breaks.
ZooKeeper stores data in a tree of paths, like a file system. Each node in the tree is a

Two flags make it useful for coordination. An ephemeral znode lives only as long as the session that created it. A sequential znode gets a 10-digit counter added to its name, such as
A session is the client's link to the cluster. If the cluster hears nothing from the client within the session
, it expires the session and deletes its ephemeral znodes.

The admin guide calls it ZAB.
A write is committed once a
of servers acknowledges it. Each change gets a zxid, a number that shows its place in the total order.
. Reads are not. Any server answers a read from its local copy, without asking a quorum.
So client A can write a value, tell client B, and B can still read the old one. The guide says B should call

A client can set a watch when it reads. A standard watch is a one-time trigger. After it fires, you must set a new one. Between the event and your next read, the znode can change again. So you cannot reliably see every change.
ZooKeeper 3.6 added persistent watches that stay after they fire.
Step through how this differs from etcd.
etcd has no tree. Keys sit in one flat, sorted key space. You read ranges of keys, so a prefix like
etcd keeps old versions of every key, which is
. A store revision counts every change to the whole key space. Each key records the revision that created it, the revision that last changed it, and a version count.

Revisions make watches stronger. You can watch a key or range from any revision still in history. Events arrive ordered by revision, and none are dropped inside the history window. A broken watch can resume just after the last revision you saw, if that revision is still in history.

This plays the role of ZooKeeper's ephemeral znodes.
A Txn is an atomic if/then/else. If every compare is true, the success operations run; otherwise the failure ones do.

instead. One member answers it from its local copy, which is faster but may be stale.
etcd rejects any request over 1.5 MiB by default. ZooKeeper checks that a znode holds less than 1 MB.
etcd's default storage limit is 2 GiB, and 8 GiB is the suggested maximum.
Past the quota, the cluster raises an alarm and accepts only reads and deletes.

Old revisions stay until you compact them. Compaction leaves gaps inside the database file, so deleting data does not shrink it on disk. Defragmentation gives the space back, but it blocks reads and writes on that member while it runs.
Roblox's BoltDB log store shows how far a file can drift from its data: 4.2 GB on disk for 489 MB of data.
A majority must write every request to disk. If those writes take too long,
can time out and start an election.
ZooKeeper also syncs each write to its log on disk before it answers, and wants a dedicated log device.
If many clients watch the same znode, one change wakes all of them, but only one can act. The recipes avoid this by having each client watch only the node just before its own.
proxy merges many watchers of one key into a single watcher on the server.

Kafka used to keep its cluster metadata in ZooKeeper. KIP-500 listed the costs. Operators had to run a second system with its own config and tools. After an election, a new controller had to load all state from ZooKeeper, which took a long time. KIP-500 also wanted Kafka to support more
The fix stores metadata as a log inside Kafka.
. Kafka 4.0, from March 2025, is the first major release that runs entirely without ZooKeeper.

c.v: "Is this coordination data, or just data?"
If it is large, changes often, or only one service reads it, move it to a database.
Count who depends on the cluster. Split critical users into their own clusters before an outage forces you to, as Roblox did afterwards.
Keep monitoring off the cluster it watches.

q.v: A ZooKeeper client sets a standard watch on /config. The node changes three times quickly. What does the client learn?

options.v: It gets three events, one per change, each with the new data.
It may get only one event. When it reads again, it sees the latest value and may have missed the changes in between.
It gets no event, because watches only fire when a node is deleted.

why.v: A standard watch is a one-time trigger. Between the event and the next read with a new watch, more changes can happen unseen.

q.v: Client A writes /flag in ZooKeeper, then tells client B to read it. B is connected to a different server and reads the old value. Is this a bug?

options.v: Yes. ZooKeeper writes are linearizable, so every read must see them.
No. Reads are served by the local server and can be stale. B should call sync() before reading.
No. ZooKeeper only promises that writes are stored on one server.

why.v: Writes are linearizable, but reads are answered locally without a quorum. The Programmer's Guide gives exactly this case.

q.v: Your team wants to store 3 MB build artifacts in etcd "because it is already there". What happens?

options.v: It works, but each write is slower.
It is rejected. By default, etcd refuses any request larger than 1.5 MiB.
etcd splits the value across members automatically.

why.v: The default request size limit is 1.5 MiB. Even smaller blobs would fill the 2 GiB default storage limit quickly.

q.v: An etcd cluster raises the space quota alarm. What still works until you fix it?

options.v: Everything. The alarm is only a warning.

why.v: The cluster goes into maintenance mode. You compact, defragment and disarm the alarm to accept writes again.

q.v: Two app servers must not process the same order at the same time. The orders live in Postgres. What is the simplest safe choice?

options.v: Add an etcd cluster and take a lock per order.
Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the order row inside the transaction that changes it.
Store a "locked" flag in a local file on each server.

why.v: The lock lives in the same database and transaction as the data, so there is no second system to fail or to fall out of step.
